introduction: On this Sunday, Moses prays with his arms raised during Israel's battle, and when he grows tired, Aaron and Hur hold up his hands. In the Gospel, Jesus tells the parable of the persistent widow who keeps asking an unjust judge for justice, to teach us to pray always and not lose heart. Paul reminds Timothy that all Scripture is inspired by God. Let us pray with perseverance.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, our help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. Let us bring him our prayers with perseverance.
intentions: For the Church: that she may pray always and never lose heart. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are denied justice: that God may defend them and that their cause may be heard. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who grow tired in prayer or in their struggles: that others may hold up their hands, as Aaron and Hur did for Moses. Let us pray to the Lord.
For preachers and teachers of the faith: that they may proclaim the word in season and out of season. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that when the Son of Man comes, he may find faith in us. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you hear the cry of your chosen ones day and night. Teach us to pray always and not lose heart, and strengthen our faith until your Son comes. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Pray always and do not lose heart
reflection.body:
In the first reading, Israel is fighting the Amalekites. Moses stands on a hill holding the staff of God. "When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed. When he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed." As the day goes on, Moses' arms grow heavy. So Aaron and Hur sit him on a stone and hold up his hands, one on each side, "until sunset."

This is a picture of prayer. Prayer can be tiring, and we cannot always sustain it alone. We need others to hold up our hands, and we can hold up theirs. The Church is a community of people who pray for one another.

Luke introduces the Gospel parable with its purpose: Jesus told it "that they must always pray and not give up." A widow keeps coming to a judge who "didn't fear God and didn't respect man," asking for justice. He refuses for a while. But in the end he gives in, simply because she keeps coming: "because this widow bothers me, I will defend her."

Jesus is not comparing God to the unjust judge. He is contrasting them. If even a corrupt judge gives in to persistence, "Won't God avenge his chosen ones who are crying out to him day and night?" God is not reluctant. But we need to keep praying, because prayer changes us and keeps our faith alive.

Then Jesus asks a sobering question: "Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?" Persistent prayer is how faith is kept alive.

Paul gives Timothy the tool for this perseverance: the Scriptures, "God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness."

This week, choose one intention you have stopped praying for, and take it up again every day. And offer to pray for someone who is tired, as Aaron and Hur held up Moses' hands.
